t: The LORD's name and the prophet's word
p: The divine name is written "the LORD" in this Plain; "the word of the LORD" opens a prophet's book.
b: The Hebrew has the four letters YHWH, the personal name of Israel's God, which Jewish readers did not say aloud and which most English Bibles print as "the LORD" in capitals. "God" (Elohim) is the common word for God or gods, and in this book the difference matters: the sailors call on "gods" (1:5), the Ninevites believe "God" (3:5), and the narrator uses both names together in 4:6. "The word of the LORD came to" is the standard opening of a prophet's message (Hosea 1:1; Joel 1:1; Micah 1:1). Jonah is the only one of the Twelve that opens this way and then tells a story, not a collection of speeches.

p: The one other place that names this prophet puts him in the northern kingdom, in the days of Jeroboam II.
b: Outside this book Jonah appears once. 2 Kings 14:25 says the LORD spoke by "Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher" and that Jeroboam II won back Israel's border. Gath-hepher lay in Galilee, in Zebulun's land (Joshua 19:13). Jeroboam II ruled about 793 to 753 BC, when Assyria was weak and Israel prospered, so the story is set in the 700s BC, a generation or two before Assyria destroyed Samaria. The name Yonah means "dove"; compare Hosea 7:11, where Ephraim is "a dove: silly, no mind of its own." "Amittai" comes from the root for "truth" or "faithfulness." Jerome reports a Hebrew tradition that Jonah was the widow of Zarephath's son whom Elijah raised (1 Kings 17:17-24). The Bible says nothing of this; it is a later legend.

p: The Hebrew word gadol, "great," is the book's thread: great city, great wind, great fear, great fish, great joy.
b: Listen for gadol. Nineveh is "the great city" (1:2; 3:2; 4:11; and 3:3, "great in God's eyes"). Then come a great wind and a great storm (1:4, 12), great fear twice (1:10, 16), a great fish (1:17, which this Plain renders "a huge fish" to match the site's fixed wording), the greatest and least of Nineveh (3:5), the king's great men (3:7), Jonah's great evil (4:1) and his great joy (4:6). The word slides from size to danger to feeling. The Plain keeps "great" wherever English allows, so the reader hears it too. Literary readers (Magonet, Sasson, Trible) treat repetition like this as the book's main way of making a point without a sermon.

p: Nineveh was the last great capital of Assyria, on the Tigris. Its fall in 612 BC ended an empire.
b: Nineveh stood on the east bank of the Tigris, across from modern Mosul in Iraq. Genesis 10:11-12 says it was built by Nimrod, who went out from Shinar (Babylonia) to Assyria, and calls the group of cities there "the great city." It became Assyria's capital under Sennacherib, who ruled from about 705 BC, and its walls enclosed a very large area (excavators give roughly 700 hectares, about 1,700 acres). Babylonians and Medes destroyed it in 612 BC; the prophet Nahum celebrates the fall. Jonah is set earlier, in the 700s BC, when Assyria was Israel's frightening neighbor. No Assyrian text mentions a Hebrew prophet or a city-wide repentance, and the book does not name the king (see 3:6).

a: wickedness has come up in front of me
p: The wording echoes God's "going down to see" Sodom (Genesis 18:20-21); the Greek makes the link plainer.
b: "Come up before me" is the language of an outcry that reaches God, as at Sodom, where the LORD says he will go down and see whether things are "as bad as the outcry that has reached me" (Genesis 18:21). The Greek text of Jonah adds the word "cry" here (see the variant). The Hebrew ra'ah means both "wickedness" and "disaster," and the book plays on that: Nineveh's ra'ah (1:2) brings a threatened ra'ah (3:10), the sailors face a ra'ah of their own (1:7-8), the Ninevites turn from their "evil way" (3:8, 10), and Jonah finds God's mercy "a great evil" (4:1). The Plain uses "wickedness" and "evil" for people's ra'ah, "disaster" for the storm, "harm" for what the LORD plans (as in Jeremiah and Joel) and "misery" in 4:6, and names the link each time.

a: run away from the LORD's presence
p: The text does not say until 4:2. Readers have given several reasons, and each changes how the whole book sounds.
b: The narrator gives no reason at first. When Jonah speaks of it in 4:2, he says he knew God would forgive. Readers fill the gap in several ways. (1) Jewish tradition: the Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael says Jonah went outside the land, where the divine presence does not come to a prophet, and feared that the Gentiles would repent and shame Israel; Rashi repeats this. (2) Jerome reports that Jonah feared being called a false prophet if the city was spared. (3) Modern readers see fear of Assyria's cruelty, or anger that a hated enemy could be forgiven. (4) Others read it as plain rebellion. Psalm 139:7-12 asks where one could flee from God and answers: nowhere. "From before the LORD" can also mean from God's service, as a prophet "stands before" the LORD (1 Kings 17:1).

p: Tarshish is a far western place, the opposite direction from Nineveh. Its exact site is debated.
b: Nineveh lay far to the east of Israel; Tarshish was as far in the other direction as a ship could go. The Bible knows Tarshish as a source of silver and metals reached by sea (1 Kings 10:22; Jeremiah 10:9; Ezekiel 27:12; Psalm 72:10), and Isaiah 23:1 calls Tyre's trading ships "ships of Tarshish." Most scholars place it in the far west, and Tartessos in southern Spain is the commonest guess. Others point to Sardinia or to north Africa. Josephus took it to be Tarsus in Cilicia (Antiquities 1.6.1). The book needs only that it is as far away as the sea goes. The Greek spells it "Tharsis."
r: 1 Kings 10:22; Jeremiah 10:9; Ezekiel 27:12; Psalm 72:10; Isaiah 23:1; Psalm 48:7

p: Jonah goes down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into its depths, and later down to the roots of the mountains.
b: The Hebrew verb yarad, "go down," marks Jonah's path: down to Joppa and down into the ship (1:3), down into the ship's deepest part (1:5), and down to where the mountains end (2:6). Its opposite is "get up" (qum) in 1:2 and 1:3, and "brought up" in 2:6. Joppa (modern Jaffa) was the main port of Judah and the central coast. Much later Peter was staying there when he was sent to a Gentile, Cornelius (Acts 10:5-9, 28), a link many readers have noticed.

p: The verb tul, "hurl," is used of the LORD's wind, the sailors' cargo, and Jonah. It shows who is really in charge.
b: The same verb tul comes four times: the LORD hurls the wind (1:4), the sailors hurl the cargo (1:5), Jonah tells them to hurl him (1:12), and they do (1:15). In 2:3 Jonah says to God, "You threw me," and the Hebrew changes to a different verb of throwing (shalakh), which the Plain marks by changing from "hurled" to "threw." The point is a chain of control: the storm is the LORD's, the sailors' desperate act answers it, and Jonah comes to see that all of it is God's doing. The Hebrew also says the ship "thought" it would break (the Plain says "seemed about to break apart"). Even the ship has more sense of danger than the prophet below deck.

a: Each man cried for help to his own god
p: The crew are probably from different peoples, and each prays to his own god.
b: Ships on the Mediterranean carried mixed crews, and each sailor had his own gods. The picture is of practical religion: they pray, they lighten the ship, then they look for the cause. The narrator treats them kindly throughout. They fear, pray, row, question and in the end turn to the LORD (1:14-16), which is more than Jonah has done. The verb za'aq, "cry for help," is the one used when Israel cried out in Egypt (Exodus 2:23).

t: The prophet asleep, the pagan awake
p: The captain's rebuke is the book's first irony: the foreigner tells the prophet to pray.
b: The captain says what a prophet should say to a frightened crew, "Call to your god," and says it to the prophet. The Hebrew word for Jonah's sleep (radam) is the deep sleep God put on Adam (Genesis 2:21) and in which Sisera lay when Jael came to him (Judges 4:21). Readers have taken it as exhaustion, as a clear conscience, as numbness after his flight, or as a refusal to face God. Jesus also slept in a boat in a storm (Mark 4:38), but there his disciples are the frightened ones and his sleep is trust, a contrast many readers draw.

t: "Perhaps the god will turn his mind to us"
p: The rare verb yit'asheth is hard. It seems to mean "give thought to," and "the god" could also be read "God."
b: The verb occurs only here and is uncertain. The Greek renders it "save us"; modern translations go with "take notice," "give a thought" or "remember." The Hebrew ha'elohim with the article can mean "the god" (the one who rules this storm) or "God." The captain's "perhaps" (ulay) is the first of several hopes uttered by non-Israelites: the king of Nineveh says "Who knows?" (3:9). Neither claims to know the god's mind, yet both are right to hope.

p: Lots asked a god who was to blame. The sailors' lot falls on Jonah, and the narrator shows the LORD steering it.
b: Lots (small marked stones or sticks) were tossed to settle questions across the ancient world. In Israel they found Achan (Joshua 7:14-18), Jonathan (1 Samuel 14:41-42) and the apostle Matthias (Acts 1:26). Proverbs 16:33 says the verdict of the lot comes from the LORD. The sailors, who do not worship him, use their own method, and it points exactly. The narrator does not argue that their method is good; he lets the LORD use it. The scrolls 4Q76, 4Q81, 4Q82 and Mur88 preserve all or part of this verse and agree with the Masoretic Text apart from spelling (4Q76 writes "lots" without the vowel letter waw) and a few small forms listed in the book introduction.

a: Which country is yours, and which people do you belong to?
p: The sailors ask a string of questions. Jonah answers one, and answers it with a creed.
b: The sailors ask about the cause of the disaster, then his work, origin, country and people. They are trying to learn whose god is angry. Jonah answers only the last question, and he does it with a creed (next verse) that overshoots what they asked. The scroll 4QXIIa (4Q76) reads "because of whom" (bishlemi, as in 1:7) where the Masoretic Text has "on whose account" (ba'asher lemi); the sense is the same, and 4QXIIf (4Q81) agrees with the Masoretic Text. Several literary critics note that Jonah gives his identity in one word, "Hebrew," and never says he is a prophet.

a: The LORD is the one I fear, the God of the heavens
p: Jonah's one statement of faith is true and ironic: he fears the God who made the sea, and he is running across it.
b: "The God of the heavens" is a title used in the Persian period for the God of Israel (Ezra 1:2; Nehemiah 1:4; Daniel 2:18), and it appears in Genesis 24:3, 7 as well. It is one of the language features critics cite for a late date for the book (see the book introduction). Jonah's creed names the LORD as maker of "the sea and the dry land" (compare Psalm 95:5). The irony is plain: he says he "fears" (yare') the LORD, yet only the sailors, in 1:10 and 1:16, show real fear. The Hebrew verb for "fear" (yare') runs through the chapter: the sailors fear the storm (1:5), Jonah says he fears the LORD (1:9), and they fear "a great fear" at his answer (1:10) and again at the calm (1:16).

p: The same Hebrew word yare' is used of terror at the storm, the creed, and worship of the LORD.
b: The Hebrew says the men "feared a great fear," which is awkward in English; the Plain says "were filled with great fear." The phrase comes again at 1:16 with the LORD as its object, so that the same words describe their terror and their worship. Their question, "What is this you have done?" (mah zo't 'asita), is the exact Hebrew of God's question to Eve in Genesis 3:13 ("What have you done here?") and of Pharaoh to Abram (Genesis 12:18). The narrator adds that Jonah "had told them" he was fleeing. The text has not said when: perhaps at the dock, when he bought passage.

a: Pick me up and hurl me into the sea
t: Why does Jonah ask to be thrown in?
p: The prophet offers his own life. Readers have taken it as courage, as death-seeking, or as a bargain with God.
b: Jonah does not repent or pray. He tells the sailors the one thing that will save them, and the cost is his life. Jewish and Christian readers have mostly admired it: the Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael counts Jonah among those who gave themselves up for God's honor, and Christian preachers have seen a figure of Christ giving his life for others. Other readers hear a man who would rather die than obey (he asks for death again in 4:3, 8). The text allows both. The sailors do not do it at once; they row against the storm first (1:13).

t: The sailors try to save him
p: The verb chatar means "dig" and is used of tunneling through a wall. The crew pull as hard as they can.
b: The Hebrew chatar elsewhere means to dig or break through (Ezekiel 8:8; Job 24:16; Amos 9:2). Here it pictures oars biting into water as the sailors try to reach shore. The detail matters: these foreign sailors do not take advantage of the prophet's offer. They hesitate to kill a man, though the lot and his own words point to him. Readers often set their decency against the sullen silence of the prophet.

t: The sailors pray to the LORD
p: A foreign crew pray to the LORD by name, and use the law's words for innocent blood.
b: For the first time anyone speaks to the LORD by name in the story, and it is the sailors. "Innocent blood" is the language of Israel's law for killing a person who has done nothing deserving death, and for the guilt that rests on a land (Deuteronomy 21:8; Jeremiah 26:15). They are afraid that if they throw Jonah in, they commit murder; if they do not, they die. Their prayer ends by saying that the LORD does as he wishes, which is the point of the whole chapter. Compare Psalm 115:3 and 135:6. 4QXIIf (4Q81) preserves most of this verse and agrees with the Masoretic Text; Mur88 differs only in spelling ("innocent" is spelled with a final aleph in the Masoretic Text and without it in Mur88).

a: filled with great fear of the LORD
p: They sacrifice and make vows. The text stops there. Readers disagree on whether this is conversion.
b: The Hebrew says they "feared the LORD a great fear" and made a sacrifice and vows. In the Hebrew Bible, "fearing the LORD" is the mark of someone who serves him, and Jonah just used the word of himself (1:9). But a sacrifice on board ship, with vows to be kept later, is odd, and some commentators think the crew only add the LORD to their gods. The later Jewish retelling in Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer makes them full converts (they throw their idols into the sea and are circumcised); that is a later legend, not in the text. Whatever the sailors become, they are the first non-Israelites in the book to turn to the LORD, and they do it before Jonah has said a word to God.

p: Hebrew dag gadol is simply "a great fish." The Greek ketos, "sea monster," is the source of "whale."
b: Hebrew dag is any fish (the same word as in Genesis 1:26); gadol is "great" (see 1:2). The book never says "whale." The Greek Old Testament says ketos, a "sea monster," and the Gospel of Matthew uses ketos in 12:40, so "whale" came into English through the Latin cetus and the King James Version. Josephus (Antiquities 9.10.2) also says the prophet was swallowed by a ketos. The Plain fixes "a huge fish" for Jonah, and keeps "sea monster" in Matthew 12:40 because that Greek word means more than "fish." Whether the Hebrew writer meant a particular animal is not known; the point of the story is that it was appointed.

p: The Hebrew manah means to assign or ordain. God appoints a fish, a plant, a worm, a wind.
b: The Hebrew manah, "appoint," appears four times in this book: the LORD appoints the fish (1:17), the plant (4:6), the worm (4:7) and the east wind (4:8). It is the verb used when a king assigns a portion or an officer (Daniel 1:5, 10, 11, 18). The fish, plant, worm and wind obey at once. Only the human characters resist. Readers have long noted that the pattern is a quiet joke at Jonah's expense.

p: The Hebrew Bible counts this verse as the first of chapter 2, so chapter 2 has ten verses here and eleven there.
b: In printed Hebrew Bibles, this sentence is Jonah 2:1, and chapter 1 has 16 verses. The English versions (and this site) put it at the end of chapter 1. So English 2:1-10 is Hebrew 2:2-11. Jewish commentaries and the Greek (which follows the Hebrew numbering in Swete's text) use the Hebrew numbers. The site gives every verse by its English number; the Hebrew number is in the data, and this note and the book introduction record the map. The Greek of Jonah 2 has the same count, 11 verses, so Swete's "2:1" is English 1:17.
orig: וַיְמַן ... לִבְלֹעַ (vayman ... livlo'a), 'and he appointed ... to swallow'

p: Jesus names Jonah's three days as the one sign he will give. Readers differ on what the sign is.
b: Jesus says "no sign except the sign of Jonah" and explains: "Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster. In the same way the Son of Man will spend three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matthew 12:40). Luke gives the sign a different sense: "Jonah became a sign for the people of Nineveh" (Luke 11:30), his preaching being the sign. Christians from Justin Martyr on have read the fish as a figure of the tomb; Jewish readers read the story as a prayer of rescue from Sheol (2:2-6). "Three days and three nights" in Hebrew idiom can mean a third day: compare 1 Samuel 30:12-13, "three days and three nights" for a man who had been left sick "three days ago." Hosea 6:2 and Esther 4:16 with 5:1 speak of three days with "on the third day."
r: Matthew 12:39-41; Matthew 16:4; Luke 11:29-32; 1 Samuel 30:12-13; Esther 4:16; Esther 5:1; Hosea 6:2

a: For three days and three nights
t: "Three days and three nights" as an idiom
p: In Hebrew and Greek counting, a part of a day counted as a day. The phrase need not mean 72 hours.
b: Ancient counting included the first and last parts of a day. The Egyptian slave left behind by his master "had gone three days and three nights without eating bread or drinking water," and then says "Three days ago I fell sick" (1 Samuel 30:12-13). Esther tells her people to fast "three days, night and day" and goes in to the king "on the third day" (Esther 4:16; 5:1). The phrase therefore can mean parts of three calendar days. Others read it literally as 72 hours, as the Greek in Matthew 12:40 invites. This matters for the Good Friday to Sunday count, which is why the debate is old (see the traditions card on this verse).

a: Jonah prayed to the LORD his God
t: A psalm of thanks in the belly of a fish
p: The prayer gives thanks for a rescue not yet complete. Scholars debate whether it belongs to the original story.
b: Jonah's first words to God are a song of thanks, not a cry for help, and they are spoken before the fish releases him (2:10). Some read the tension as the point: Jonah speaks of rescue in the past tense because he is sure of it, or because this is what he prayed in the fish and the narrator gives the poem as he later told it. Many critical commentators (for example Wolff) think the psalm was inserted later, partly because it contains no repentance and no mention of the sea storm as punishment; others (Landes, Magonet, Sasson, Trible) argue it fits the story's irony and is original. The Greek and the Hebrew both have it. Mur88 preserves 2:1 and much of the psalm, and 4QXIIg (4Q82) preserves parts of 2:2-9.

a: I called to the LORD out of my trouble
p: Almost every line of Jonah's prayer echoes the Psalms. It is a mosaic, not a new poem.
b: The line echoes Psalm 120:1 almost word for word, and the pattern of "I called ... and he answered" belongs to the thanksgiving psalms (Psalm 18:6; Psalm 30:2; Psalm 34:4). Other echoes in this prayer: 2:3 and Psalm 42:7; 2:4 and Psalm 31:22; 2:5 and Psalm 69:1-2; 2:6 and Psalm 30:3; 2:8 and Psalm 31:6; 2:9 and Psalm 50:14 and Psalm 3:8. Commentators (Sasson, Limburg) note that this is how a trained worshipper would pray: he reaches for words he has sung before. Readers who find the prayer too polished for a man in a fish note this; readers who see it as the book's irony say Jonah is pious in words and blind in practice.
r: Psalm 120:1; Psalm 18:6; Psalm 30:2; Psalm 42:7; Psalm 31:22; Psalm 69:1-2; Psalm 31:6; Psalm 50:14; Psalm 3:8

p: Jonah calls the fish "the belly of Sheol," the world of the dead. He speaks as a man already given up for dead.
b: The word for "belly" is beten, a different word from the "insides" (me'im) of the fish in 1:17 and 2:1. Jonah speaks as if he were already in Sheol: the Hebrew word for the place of the dead, which in the Psalms is entered by drowning or sickness (Psalm 30:3; Psalm 88:5-6). For a man who was thrown into the sea, the picture fits: the water that closed over him was Sheol's door. The prayer does not say "I am in a fish" at all; the fish is told only by the narrator. Later readers have used "Sheol" here for the Christian reading of the sign of Jonah (descent to the dead).
orig: מִבֶּטֶן שְׁאוֹל (mibbeten she'ol), 'from the belly of Sheol'

a: You threw me into the deep
p: Jonah gives God the credit for the throw. The sailors threw him, but Jonah says it was the LORD.
b: The sailors hurled Jonah (1:15), but Jonah says "you" did. He now sees the whole sequence as the LORD's act. The word for "deep" is metsulah, the depth where Egypt's soldiers sank (Exodus 15:5; Nehemiah 9:11). The prayer takes the chaos of the sea as the place of judgment, and takes God, not the storm, as the agent. Compare 1:4, where the LORD "hurled" the wind with a different verb (tul): the Hebrew does not repeat the word, so the Plain does not either.

p: Hebrew nahar is "river," an odd word for the sea. It echoes Sea and River, the rivals of God in older myths.
b: Nahar is a river, but in poetry about the sea it can name the great stream thought to ring the world or the deep waters under it (Psalm 24:2; Jonah 2:3). In the Ugaritic tablets (about 1400-1200 BC), "Sea" (Yam) and "River" (Nahar) are paired as rival powers whom the storm god Baal defeats. Habakkuk 3:8 asks whether the LORD's anger is "against the rivers" and "against the sea." Verdict: the Hebrew poets use the language of old combat myths, but Jonah's prayer does not retell them; "river" here is a vivid word for the currents that held him. Many translations say "current" or "flood."

p: Jonah thinks he has been cast out, as Adam and Cain were.
b: The verb garash, "drive out," is used for Adam driven out of Eden (Genesis 3:24) and Cain from the ground (Genesis 4:14). Psalm 31:22 has a similar cry, "I have been cut away from before your eyes." Jonah had tried to flee "from before the LORD" (1:3); now he sees what he feared as a punishment: God himself has driven him from his sight. Yet the next line turns.

p: Hebrew nefesh means throat, neck, life or self. Psalm 69:1 has the same words.
b: Hebrew nefesh is the throat or windpipe as well as the "life" or "soul." Psalm 69:1 has the same picture, "the water has reached my throat," and Jonah 2:5 has the same words, "water ... up to the throat" (ad nefesh). Only the verb differs: Jonah has afafuni, "surrounded me," where the psalm has ba'u, "came in." The Greek renders it "soul" (psyche), "the water poured around me up to my soul." Both are true here: the water reaches the throat, and the life is at stake. The Plain says "throat" to keep the physical picture and the link to the Psalm.

p: The Hebrew qitsvey harim means the cut-off ends or foundations of the mountains, the bottom of the world.
b: The word qetsev means a cut or cut-off end, and the phrase pictures the ocean floor where the mountains stop, the foundations of the earth. Ancient Israelites thought of the mountains as rooted deep under the sea (Psalm 18:7; Job 38:6). The Greek reads "the clefts of the mountains." To go down to the mountains' roots is to go as low as the world goes.
orig: לְקִצְבֵי הָרִים (leqitsvey harim), 'to the cut-off ends of the mountains'

a: The earth with its bars was shut behind me forever
p: The bars of the earth are the gates of Sheol. Jonah is describing the world of the dead as a locked city.
b: Sheol is pictured as a walled place with gates and bars (Job 38:17; Isaiah 38:10; Psalm 107:16). In Mesopotamian myth the underworld is also a city of gates: in the story of Ishtar's descent she passes through seven, and it is called the land of no return. Verdict: Israel shared the picture with its neighbors, but nothing in Jonah borrows a particular story; the point is that the gate is locked from the outside. Only God can open it, and the next line says he has.

t: "You brought my life up from the Pit"
p: The reversal: Jonah went down; God brought him up. The words echo Psalm 30:3 and, for Christians, the resurrection.
b: The verb ala, "bring up," answers Jonah's repeated "go down" (1:3, 5; 2:6). Psalm 30:3 says almost the same thing: the LORD lifted a life out of Sheol. The Pit (shachat) is a name for the grave and Sheol (Psalm 16:10; Psalm 30:9). In the Hebrew Bible the language is of rescue from near death, not resurrection from the dead. Christian readers have heard more (Matthew 12:40), and the Yom Kippur reading of Jonah in the synagogue hears the same rescue as God's pardon.

p: Jonah prays toward the temple. It is either the temple in Jerusalem or God's heavenly dwelling.
b: "Your holy temple" (heykal qodshekha) can mean the Jerusalem temple, where Jonah, a northerner, would pray toward Jerusalem as Solomon's prayer allowed (1 Kings 8:38, 44; compare Daniel 6:10), or God's temple in heaven (Psalm 11:4). Both fit. The Hebrew verb "look toward" in 2:4 and "come to" here suggest an act of prayer in a direction. For Jonah's first readers, perhaps in Persian-period Judah, the temple was the center of prayer, and the phrase would have sounded familiar and local.

p: The phrase is the same as in Psalm 31:6: hevley shav, false gods or worthless things.
b: Hebrew havley shav is "vapors of emptiness." The site's Plain of Psalm 31:6 uses the same rendering. Elsewhere hevel is the word for idols (Deuteronomy 32:21; 2 Kings 17:15; Jeremiah 8:19) and "empty nothings" fits all of them. The line seems aimed at the sailors' gods. It sits oddly with the sailors' own conduct in chapter 1, and so some critics take it as a mark of Jonah's self-righteousness, a point the book never states but allows the reader to notice.

p: Hard Hebrew: "their loyal love they abandon." It may mean the loyalty they owe God, or the love God would show them.
b: Hebrew chasdam is literally "their loyal love." Three readings: (1) they abandon their own faithfulness to God; (2) they abandon the loyal love that is theirs to receive, that is, God himself, who is called "my loyal love" in Psalm 144:2; (3) they abandon the true source of loyal love. The Greek says "they forsook their mercy." The scroll 4QXIIg (4Q82) preserves the verse in part with fuller spellings (for example "they abandon" written with a waw), which do not change the sense. The Plain keeps the phrase close to the Hebrew and hard. See also 4:2, where Jonah says God is "great in loyal love," the same word.

p: The prayer ends with a thank offering, a vow to be kept, and the cry "Rescue is the LORD's!"
b: A "thanksgiving" (todah) is the sacrifice and song of someone who has been saved (Leviticus 7:12; Psalm 50:14; Psalm 116:17). The vow to be paid is the same kind as the sailors' vows (1:16; Psalm 116:14). The last line, "Rescue is the LORD's!", is nearly the same as the closing words of Psalm 3:8; the word "rescue" (yeshu'ah) is the one from which "Jesus" (Yeshua) is later derived. In the story, it is also a hinge: the same God who rescues Jonah rescues Nineveh, and Jonah does not like that (4:2).

a: The LORD spoke to the fish
p: The only one in the book who obeys the LORD at once is a fish.
b: The LORD "speaks" and the fish vomits; elsewhere in the book the LORD hurls a wind, appoints a plant, a worm, a wind (1:4; 4:6-8) and each does exactly what is asked. The prophet and the sailors are the only ones with a choice. The verb qi', "vomit," is blunt; the Plain keeps it. Mur88 and 4QXIIg (4Q82) both preserve this verse and agree with the Masoretic Text. Some Christian writers compare the release on dry land to resurrection; Jewish tradition more often notes the God who commands the sea.

t: A second word, a second chance
p: Jonah is sent again with no reproach. The same words as chapter 1 begin the chapter.
b: The chapter opens like chapter 1, and the second commission repeats the first nearly word for word (1:1-2; 3:1-2). There is no rebuke, no mention of the fish and no question. Some prophets in Scripture are commissioned a second time (Jeremiah 13:3). The Greek says "a second time" in the same way. The repetition is a literary signal that the story starts over, now with a prophet who obeys.

t: "Call out to" the city, not "against" it
p: In 1:2 the call is against Nineveh. Now it is to it, and the Greek says "in it."
b: Hebrew has qara' 'al, "call out against," in 1:2 and qara' 'el, "call out to," here. The two prepositions are often interchangeable in later Hebrew, so the difference may be only style, but some readers see the shift from judgment to message. The Greek says "in it," and also adds "the former announcement," as the variant shows. The "announcement" (qeri'ah) is unspecified until 3:4, as if God gives Jonah the words on the road. Jonah's whole sermon is five words in Hebrew.

t: "Nineveh was a city" in the past tense
p: The Hebrew says hayetah, "was." Critics take this as a sign that the writer looks back on a city that no longer stands.
b: The Greek also says "was" (en). Many scholars think it shows the writer looks back from a time when Nineveh was gone (after 612 BC), but the Hebrew narrator might use the past tense for any story set in the past. Together with the late-looking language of the book (see the book introduction), the tense is part of the case for a post-exilic date. Defenders of an earlier date (Stuart, Alexander) reply that the past tense fits the narrator's story about earlier events.

a: a city great in God's eyes
p: The Hebrew gadolah le'elohim can mean "very great" (God's name as a superlative) or "great in God's eyes."
b: The phrase literally says "a great city to God." Some take elohim as a superlative, as in "mountains of God" (Psalm 36:6) for very high mountains, so "enormous." Others take it as importance: Nineveh matters to God, which prepares for the end of the book (4:11). The Plain keeps the second reading in the sentence, which is close to the Hebrew, and puts the first in this note. Both are old; the Greek has "great to God."

p: The Hebrew says a walk of three days. It may mean its width, a three-day stay, or the whole Assyrian heartland.
b: Readers take it in four ways. (1) Three days' walking to cross or go around the city, a huge figure that has been compared with the walls the excavations found (about 8 miles around) and does not fit well. (2) Three days is how long it takes to visit all the city and its sites, with the "one day's walk" of 3:4 as the first third. (3) Nineveh means the whole region of the Assyrian cities (Genesis 10:11-12 names Nineveh, Rehoboth-ir, Calah and Resen), a metropolitan area many miles across. (4) A literary exaggeration to signal the city's size and importance. The Greek reads "a walk of three days" for the same words. The "one day's walk" in 3:4 supports the idea of a stay, not a diameter.

p: The Hebrew nehpakhet can mean overthrown, as Sodom was, or turned around. The pun is the whole story.
b: The verb hapakh is the one used for the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:25; Deuteronomy 29:23), and "overthrow" is the Plain's wording there. But the same verb in other contexts means to turn, to change (Exodus 7:17, 20; Psalm 114:8) and, in the passive form here, "be changed." Jonah speaks of a coming destruction; what happens is a change of heart. The word is therefore both a threat and a promise, and Nineveh is "overturned" in the second sense. Some Christian fathers, notably Augustine in The City of God 18.44, read the overthrow as the overthrow of wickedness. The Greek has "will be overthrown" (katastraphesetai).

p: The Ninevites believe in God (Elohim), not the LORD by name. The faith language is that of Abraham.
b: The verb is he'emin, "believe, trust," followed by "in" (b-), as in Genesis 15:6 (Abram trusted the LORD) and Exodus 14:31. Notice what the Ninevites say and do not say: they believe in Elohim, "God," without the personal name; so do the king and the narrator in this scene. Jonah's five-word message does not say "repent" or name any offer of mercy, so their faith is a response to the threat and a hope (3:9). Jesus later says that the people of Nineveh "repented" at Jonah's preaching (Matthew 12:41).

p: A fast, sackcloth and ashes were the standard way a community showed mourning and begged for mercy.
b: Fasting by a whole community in a crisis is well attested in the Bible (1 Kings 21:27; Joel 1:14; Joel 2:15-16; Esther 4:3, 16). Sackcloth (rough cloth, often goat's hair) and ashes were the clothing of grief. Here the whole city does it "from the greatest to the least," the Plain's wording of the Hebrew "from their great ones to their small ones," again the book's word gadol. The Ninevites repent in the Israelite way: fast, sackcloth, prayer and turning from violence. The book does not say that they learned this from Jonah.

a: When word reached the king of Nineveh
p: The king is not named. No Assyrian record tells of such a king in sackcloth.
b: Jonah's king is not named, and the book calls him "the king of Nineveh," not "the king of Assyria," a title Assyrian kings would use. Some think this is a deliberate lack of historical detail (a literary story), others that the writer used the title the Israelites used of a king in his capital (compare "the king of Samaria" in 1 Kings 21:1). Assyrian kings were known for rituals to avert bad omens, including putting a substitute on the throne while the real king stayed hidden; commentators sometimes compare this to the king's humbling, but no text connects the two. Other kings in the Bible respond to a prophet's word in similar ways (Ahab in 1 Kings 21:27-29; Hezekiah in 2 Kings 19:1).

p: The decree makes animals fast and wear sackcloth. This has parallels, but the idea is startling.
b: The order covers "human being and animal" (ha'adam vehabbehemah), herd and flock. Animals sharing human mourning has parallels: the Persians, says Herodotus, cut the manes of their horses and pack animals in mourning for Masistius (Histories 9.24); the book of Judith has Israel putting sackcloth on cattle in prayer (Judith 4:10); and in Joel the beasts groan in the drought (Joel 1:18, 20). Some readers find it comic, a joke about what a foreigner might do; others find it moving, because it prepares for God's concern for the animals in 4:11. The Greek agrees with the Hebrew here ("his nobles" for "his great men").

a: turn back from his evil way
p: The verb shuv, "turn back," is the Bible's word for repentance. The king names the specific sin: violence.
b: Shuv, "turn back," is used here and in 3:9 and 3:10. The same words appear in Jeremiah's prophecy: "each will turn back from his evil way" (Jeremiah 36:3), and in his rule that a nation that turns back will see God change his mind (Jeremiah 18:8). The only sin the story names in Nineveh is "violence" (chamas), the word for the sin that brought the flood (Genesis 6:11, 13) and Nahum's "city of blood." The king's wording is what a prophet would say. The Greek reads "injustice."

p: The king hopes for mercy but does not presume on it. The phrase comes from David and Joel.
b: Mi yode'a means "Who knows?" It expresses a hope that the speaker has no right to claim. David uses it when his child is sick: "Who knows? The LORD might show me favor" (2 Samuel 12:22). Joel 2:14 uses nearly the same wording about the LORD's possible turning. God is free; repentance cannot force his hand. The king uses a generic word for God (ha'Elohim), and he echoes the captain's "perhaps" (1:6). The verbs "turn" (shuv) and "change his mind" (nicham) are the words of 3:10. "Burning anger" (charon 'af) is God's fierce anger as in Exodus 32:12.

a: God changed his mind about the harm
p: The Hebrew nicham is the verb of Jeremiah 18:8 and Exodus 32:14. The Plain uses the same English as Jeremiah.
b: The same verb is used when God gave up his plan to destroy Israel after the golden calf (Exodus 32:14) and in Jeremiah's rule: "I will change my mind about the harm I planned to do to it" (Jeremiah 18:8; also Jeremiah 26:3, 13, 19). The Plain uses "change his mind" in all of them. The word does not mean regret for a mistake. It describes God's response to people's turning, and the sentence puts it next to the people's turning ("they turned back," 3:10). Whether this means God really changes or speaks to us in human terms is debated; see the topic and the traditions card here. The "harm" (ra'ah) is the same word as the Ninevites' "evil" (3:8, 10), and the Plain follows Jeremiah in calling it "harm" when the LORD plans it.
r: Exodus 32:14; Jeremiah 18:8; Jeremiah 18:10; Jeremiah 26:3; Jeremiah 26:13; Jeremiah 26:19; Joel 2:13

p: Jonah said Nineveh would be overturned, and it was not. The Bible has a rule for this.
b: Deuteronomy 18:22 says a prophet whose word does not come true is not speaking for the LORD ("that is a word the LORD has not spoken"). Jonah's word did not come true. The Bible gives the answer in Jeremiah 18:7-10: a message of disaster is conditional, and a nation's turning cancels it. Jonah's five words contain no condition, and that is why he is angry (4:2). Another answer: the word came true in the second sense of "overturned" (3:4). Jewish and Christian readers have noted that this is a prophet who is proved "false" by God's mercy; Jerome says that is what Jonah feared.

p: The Hebrew uses the book's word ra'ah, "evil," for what Jonah feels. God's mercy is a ra'ah to him.
b: Literally the Hebrew says "it was evil to Jonah, a great evil," and then "he burned" (charah). God relented from a ra'ah (3:10) and now Jonah experiences a ra'ah: the word has passed from Nineveh's wickedness (1:2) to the disaster God held back (3:10) to Jonah's distress. Translations soften it to "displeased" or "seemed very wrong." The Plain keeps the word so that the reader sees it. The Greek has "grief" (lype) and says he "was troubled." Notice also "great" again: a great evil, and later a great joy (4:6). The Hebrew does not say "great anger"; "he burned" has no "great" in front of it.
orig: וַיֵּרַע אֶל־יוֹנָה רָעָה גְדוֹלָה (vayyera' el-Yonah ra'ah gedolah)

a: That is why I hurried to flee to Tarshish
p: Only here does Jonah say why he ran. Readers see fear of being called false, protest, or pride.
b: Jonah says he fled because he knew the LORD would forgive. Jerome says Jonah feared being thought a false prophet (see 3:10). The Mekhilta tradition says he feared Israel would be shamed by a repentant Gentile city (1:3). Modern commentators add: (1) many commentators read the book as a challenge to narrow views of God's mercy; (2) some hear a protest against God's lack of justice, since he forgives Assyria, which will destroy Israel; (3) Jonah knows his own creed too well to want to preach it to an enemy. The surprising part is that the creed is correct; the Hebrew reads as if Jonah expected a God like this and wanted one stricter.

a: a God gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and great in loyal love
p: This is the creed of Exodus 34:6-7, the way Joel 2:13 and several psalms repeat it. Jonah turns it into a complaint.
b: The creed is the LORD's own self-description at Sinai: "compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). It is repeated in Numbers 14:18, Nehemiah 9:17 ("gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and great in loyal love"), Psalm 86:15, Psalm 103:8, Psalm 145:8 and Joel 2:13. Jonah has the order of Nehemiah and Psalm 145:8 (gracious, then compassionate), drops "faithfulness," and omits the warning clause of Exodus 34:7 about guilt not being left unpunished. He adds "changes his mind about the harm," which Joel 2:13 also adds in the same words. The Plain keeps "loyal love" (hesed) as in Exodus 34. The same words that Moses heard as grace, Jonah hears as scandal.
r: Exodus 34:6; Exodus 34:7; Numbers 14:18; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalm 86:15; Psalm 103:8; Psalm 145:8; Joel 2:13

a: one who changes his mind about the harm
p: The last item in Jonah's creed is the one that matters to his case. It is not in Exodus 34.
b: This is the clause not found in Exodus 34:6-7. Joel 2:13 adds the same words. The Plain uses "changes his mind" here, as in 3:10, so that readers can see that the thing Jonah complains about in 4:2 is what the narrator said in 3:10. In Jeremiah, the same attribute explains why a prophet's warnings are conditional (Jeremiah 18:7-10). The topic page on God changing his mind sets out how Jews and Christians have read this.

a: please take my life from me
p: Jonah echoes Elijah's prayer, but with the opposite occasion.
b: Elijah said "Now, LORD, take my life" (1 Kings 19:4) when his work had apparently failed; Moses said something close when the burden of Israel was too great (Numbers 11:15), and Jeremiah and Job wished they had never been born (Jeremiah 20:14-18; Job 3). Jonah says it because his work succeeded. The Plain gives "my death is better than my life," which keeps the Hebrew words tov mavti mechayyai, repeated in 4:8. The result is a comic and sad echo: Jonah wants to die because Nineveh will live.

a: Are you right to burn with anger?
p: The Hebrew hetev can mean "rightly" or "very." God's question is the one Jonah has to answer.
b: The adverb hetev means "well, rightly." "Are you right to be angry?" (the Plain) takes it that way. The Greek understood it as "very": "Are you very grieved?" (sphodra lelypesai). The first reading makes God's question a challenge, the second a gentle question about Jonah's feeling. The same phrase returns in 4:9, where Jonah answers "I am right to burn with anger, even to death." God does not argue the point; he asks, and Jonah leaves.

p: A sukkah is a rough shelter of branches, the kind of hut a watchman or harvester uses.
b: The Hebrew sukkah is a booth of leafy branches, like the booths of the Feast of Booths and a watchman's hut in a vineyard (Isaiah 1:8). Jonah sits outside the city, waiting. Why he waits is not said. Most take it that he still expects the city to be destroyed after the forty days. Some readers have suggested that this scene comes during the forty days, before the Ninevites repent in chapter 3. A neat twist: the booth he makes fails him, and the LORD gives him a better one.

p: The plant is meant to rescue Jonah from his ra'ah. The word means evil, disaster, or trouble.
b: The word ra'ah (see 1:2) appears again: the plant is to rescue Jonah "from his ra'ah" (the Plain says "misery"). It is his bad mood and the heat, but the word reminds the reader of the larger "evil" and "disaster." The Greek reads "from his evils" (ton kakon). Jonah's "rescue" by a plant mirrors his rescue by a fish (2:6) if the Masoretic Text's hatsil, "rescue," is the right reading. One scroll (4Q82) and the Greek instead have "to shade him," which would remove the mirror (see the variant at 4:6). The word "rejoice" (samach) is used of his joy.

a: Jonah rejoiced over the plant with great joy
t: Claude's theory: the plant is a second fish
p: The plant plays the part the fish played in chapter 2. Both rescue Jonah, and each rescue is undone by God to teach him.
b: This is my own reading, and it depends on the Masoretic Text's "rescue" in 4:6; if 4Q82 and the Greek ("to shade him") are right, the plant only shades and the parallel with the fish is weaker. It overlaps with the literary readings of Magonet and Trible, who note that chapters 1-2 and 3-4 mirror each other. The fish saved Jonah from drowning and he sang thanks; the plant saves him from heat and he is glad, for the first time in the book. But the plant is for his comfort alone, and he never says thanks. The fish was appointed to save him so that he might serve; the plant, worm and wind teach what he missed. In both pairs God uses an animal (fish, worm) to act, a way of saying that the creatures obey God and the prophet is the slow one.

p: The east wind (the sirocco) came from the desert and withered crops. The adjective charishit is a rare word.
b: The east wind from the desert is a destructive wind in the Bible (Genesis 41:6; Exodus 14:21; Psalm 48:7; Ezekiel 19:12; Hosea 12:1). The adjective charishit appears only here. It may mean "scorching" or "sultry," from a root for being silent or still (a heavy, oppressive heat), or from "plowing," for a wind that cuts. The Greek renders it "scorching" (kausonos). The Plain says "hot east wind." The wind is the fourth thing the LORD "appoints" (see 1:17).

a: You had pity on the plant
t: "Pity" for a plant, "pity" for a city
p: The verb chus, "pity, spare," is used of the plant and of Nineveh. It is a different word from the "compassion" of 4:2.
b: Chus is the feeling that holds back harm to something because it is valuable or helpless. Jonah "had pity" on a plant he did not plant, water or watch grow, which lived "in one night" and perished in one. God asks how much more should he "have pity" on a city with a hundred and twenty thousand people and animals. The argument is from lesser to greater, a pattern the rabbis later named qal vachomer. The verb in the creed (rachum, "compassionate") is another word: the Plain keeps them apart.

a: more than 120,000 people who do not know the difference between their right hand and their left
p: They are either small children or all the people of Nineveh, seen as morally ignorant.
b: Two readings are old. (1) Little children, too young to know right from left: that would imply a population of several hundred thousand, with the 120,000 as the youngest (compare Deuteronomy 1:39, "your children who do not yet know good from bad"; Isaiah 7:15-16). (2) The whole population, who do not know right from left in a moral sense: they have never been taught the LORD's ways. The first fits the numbers of an enormous city; the second fits God's argument that Nineveh has not been taught as Israel was. The text does not say. Either way, God's concern is for those who do not know, the pity of a teacher for the untaught.

p: The book ends by naming animals among those God cares for.
b: The last words of the Hebrew are "and many animals" (uvehemah rabbah). The animals have been under sackcloth with the Ninevites (3:7-8) and now appear in God's own reason for mercy. Psalm 36:6 says the LORD keeps both humans and animals safe, and Psalm 104:27 says all creatures wait on him. Some read this as an ecological or creation theme. Others see an irony: God's last argument includes a detail that would have seemed unworthy of a prophet.

a: And should I not have pity on Nineveh
p: The book ends with God's question. Jonah does not reply. The reader must.
b: The story stops with a question. Jonah never answers, and the narrator never says what he does next. Readers have supplied: (1) Jonah repents (a traditional inference: the story was told, so Jonah must have told it); (2) Jonah stays sulking, and the ending warns the reader against his example; (3) the ending is open on purpose, so the reader has to decide what to do with the same question (Trible, Sasson, Limburg). The Greek and the Murabba'at scroll Mur88 both end the book where the Masoretic Text does. The Yom Kippur reading ends here too, and many communities then read Micah 7:18-20.
